rv.q: Bertie Carvel is phenomenal – a more persuasive, acute and entertaining Henry Higgins never exercised his vocal cords.
The effect of George Bernard Shaw’s play is, to me anyway, still one of delight - at its cleverness, its sense of fun and its sheer energy.
There is a thrilling, thin-ice energy to Richard Jones’s production of George Bernard Shaw’s play, a tension brilliantly embodied by leads Patsy Ferran and Bertie Carvel.
For a 110-year-old drama, it packs a mighty modern punch.
This Pygmalion may not prove universally popular — but it's very exciting and undoubtedly audacious.
I can’t think of another stage actor who changes as radically for each role as Carvel but his tour de force here left me impressed but unmoved.
We’re left with an exercise in ‘Pygmalion’ which, for all its detail, forgets about the heart, the humour and, crucially, the humanity.
But this neither feels like a faithful rendering, nor a transformation with real contemporary heft.
For now, it feels like a curious thing: a glass showcase for Carvel and Ferran to fill with towering, uneasy displays of acting elan.
But Jones’s production is pitched so high and loud that it is hard to engage with the points either he or Shaw are making.
The production feels strangely like a museum piece despite its contemporary visual elements.
The opening scene, where they meet among West End crowds in a rainstorm, is a cacophony of overblown acting and frenetic movement.
Yet, for all its fun, it unnecessarily clouds Shaw’s message with surprising oddities.
All in all, it’s an incredibly frustrating evening, a wasted revival of a play that for all its old-fashioned notions, still speaks resonantly – and impeccably – to the modern age.
On paper this show is a hit; in reality it feels like a missed opportunity to create something really special.
Despite having every opportunity, including an impressive cast, this Pygmalion can’t quite elevate its status beyond bland revival.

cn.t: Mixed reviews for this frenetic revival, with critics divided on Richard Jones's stylized direction. While Patsy Ferran and Bertie Carvel's performances earn praise, the breakneck pacing and exaggerated acting style prove polarizing.
